question: What is an immunization defaulter?

options.A: A child who misses a scheduled vaccine dose
options.B: A parent who refuses all medical treatments
options.C: A health worker who forgets to order vaccines
options.D: An infant who experiences a mild vaccine reaction

explanation: A defaulter simply refers to a child who fails to show up for a scheduled vaccine or misses a dose needed to complete their immunization schedule. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h1)

question: Why is finding immunization defaulters so important for a community?

options.A: It proves that community health workers are working hard
options.B: It helps health clinics earn more money from the government
options.C: It stops dangerous disease outbreaks by closing immunity gaps
options.D: It reduces the total number of children born each year

explanation: When children miss their shots, community immunity drops, making it easy for deadly infections to spread quickly among vulnerable infants. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h1)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common reason why caregivers miss vaccine appointments?

options.A: Free vaccine supplies available at every street corner
options.B: Long travel distances and lack of transport money
options.C: Fear of side effects and circulating community rumors
options.D: Harsh attitudes from busy health facility staff

explanation: Abundant free supplies near homes would encourage vaccination rather than cause defaulting. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h2)

question: A mother stops bringing her baby for immunizations because health workers shouted at her for arriving late last month. What type of factor caused this default?
explanation: Poor staff attitudes and hostile clinic environments are system-level barriers that drive caregivers away from health facilities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h2)

question: Where is the scheduled date for a child's next vaccine dose primarily recorded for the mother to see?

options.B: On the child's home-based health card
options.C: In the national budget allocation report
options.D: In the local government tax receipt

explanation: The child health card stays with the caregiver and serves as the primary personal reminder for upcoming immunization dates. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h3)

question: How do clinic registers help nurses identify children who have defaulted?

options.A: By calculating the exact weight the child will gain next month
options.B: By predicting which family will move to another state
options.C: By automatically ordering new vaccine vials from the depot
options.D: By tracking missed return dates between scheduled clinic visits

explanation: Facility registers record attendance dates, making it easy to see when a child fails to return for their next scheduled dose. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h3)

question: Who are local community health volunteers primarily expected to help during defaulter tracking?

options.A: Managing financial budgets for the health clinic
options.B: Prescribing complex antibiotics during home visits
options.C: Performing major surgeries in village squares
options.D: Mapping households and reporting missing infants

explanation: Volunteers live within the community, making them ideal for identifying newborn babies and locating families who missed clinic visits. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h4)

question: A community health nurse visits a home where a mother has missed two vaccine appointments. What is the best first step during the visit?

options.A: Threaten to report the family to local village authorities
options.B: Listen to the mother's reasons with empathy and offer gentle guidance
options.C: Inform the neighbors that the mother is neglecting her baby
options.D: Administer the vaccines immediately without asking any questions

explanation: A respectful, non-judgmental approach builds trust and helps uncover the real reasons behind the missed appointments. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h4)

question: What communication style should a nurse use when counseling a caregiver who defaulted on vaccines?

options.A: Total silence while the caregiver reads a pamphlet
options.B: Rapid medical terminology to prove professional status
options.C: Strict lecturing to show authority and clinical power
options.D: Respectful listening and clear, non-judgmental explanations

explanation: Caregivers respond better to patience and empathy than to strict scolding, which often makes them avoid the clinic permanently. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h5)

question: Why is it important to discover the exact reason a caregiver stopped immunizing?

options.A: It allows the nurse to give targeted and relevant solutions
options.B: It is required before ordering medical equipment from abroad
options.C: It gives the clinic grounds to fine the family for non-compliance
options.D: It helps health workers blame the community for poor statistics

explanation: Different problems need different answers—transport issues require outreach scheduling, while fear of side effects requires reassurance and health education. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h5)

question: What is the standard defaulter rate commonly measured in routine immunization programs?

options.A: The drop-out rate between the first and last doses of a series
options.B: The percentage of expired vaccine vials found in the fridge
options.C: The total number of babies born in a hospital annually
options.D: The daily count of pregnant women attending antenatal care

explanation: The drop-out rate—such as the difference between Penta 1 and Penta 3 uptake—is the standard metric used to measure defaulting. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h6)

question: Why should primary health care teams regularly review their defaulter tracing data?

options.A: To prove that no children ever miss their scheduled vaccines
options.B: To justify stopping immunization services in rural areas
options.C: To find persistent barriers and improve community outreach strategies
options.D: To punish health workers whose clinics have low coverage

explanation: Reviewing data helps health teams spot trends, fix recurring bottlenecks, and adapt their outreach to reach every child. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T74#GNS214_U1_T74_h6)
